# cancho-gateway

> An auditable HTTP/1.1 reverse proxy written in cancho: one thread, one poller, memory sized at start, every input bounded and refused by name, strict parsing against request smuggling, one JSON access-log line per request. The deployment file is compiled into the binary (one binary per deployment). Alpha: not certified for production, and slower than HAProxy on most benchmark cells and than nginx on POST bodies.

## Read first
- [Overview](https://alpibrusl.github.io/cancho-gateway/): what it is, where it fits, the numbers.
- [Evidence](https://alpibrusl.github.io/cancho-gateway/evidence.html): what each test covers, what it found, how each number was measured, what is not claimed.
- [Proof](https://alpibrusl.github.io/cancho-gateway/proof.html): the authority report the compiler derives for the binary, every label explained, and what it does not prove.
- [Lab](https://alpibrusl.github.io/cancho-gateway/lab.html): send any request head and the framing judge answers in the browser; verified against the probe's recorded answers on every load.
- [Examples and download](https://alpibrusl.github.io/cancho-gateway/examples.html): ten situations with their deployment files and what the gateway answers and logs; the demo binary from the latest release.
- [Design](https://github.com/alpibrusl/cancho-gateway/blob/main/docs/design.md): scope, the authority row, the bounds and their rule tags.

## Facts that matter when using it
- Configuration is a TOML deployment file, checked and compiled in: `python3 scripts/generate.py my.toml && cancho build`. A bad file is refused with `{file, hint, key, line, message, rule}` on stderr and exit code 2.
- Routes: the host selects the route set, then the longest segment-boundary path prefix that allows the method; a tie is a config error. A route may set `max_body` and `trust_forwarded`.
- Every refusal is `application/problem+json` with a `rule` tag (for example `framing.two-lengths`, `limit.body`, `proxy.connect`, `timeout.upstream`) and a `request_id`. The same id is in the `X-Request-Id` response header and the access log.
- The access log is JSON lines on stdout: `t, id, method, path (no query string), route, upstream, status, rule, outcome, ms, upstream_ms, bytes_in, bytes_out`, then `tls`, `upgrade`, `identity` and `ws_close` when they apply. A stdout reader that stops stalls the gateway.
- Optional admin port (`admin_listen`): `/metrics` (JSON, or Prometheus text with `?format=prometheus`), `/healthz`, `/readyz` (503 with the reasons as data). It binds every interface and has no authentication: firewall it.
- Headers: hop-by-hop headers are removed; `Via`, `X-Forwarded-Host` and `X-Forwarded-Proto` are added; a client's `Forwarded`, `X-Forwarded-*`, `X-Real-IP` and `X-Request-Id` are not believed unless the route sets `trust_forwarded = true`. There is no `X-Forwarded-For` of the gateway's own: the compiler gives no client address.
- WebSocket (OCPP-J between chargers and a back office): a route sets `websocket = true`, `subprotocols = ["ocpp1.6"]`, `origins = [...]`. The opening handshake is checked and refused by name (`ws.*` rule tags), the upstream's `101` is checked (including `Sec-WebSocket-Accept`), and the connection then becomes a tunnel with an idle timeout and a lifetime (`ws_idle_timeout_ms`, `ws_max_lifetime_ms`, `ws_max_tunnels`). The gateway reads the frames of the tunnel in both directions (docs/websocket-frames.md): a violation of RFC 6455 section 5, a message over the route's `ws_max_message_bytes` (default 1048576, 1024 to 268435456) or invalid UTF-8 in a text message is answered with a Close frame (1002, 1009, 1007; 1011 to a client whose upstream broke the rules) and the tunnel is closed, with a rule tag `ws.frame-*`, `ws.message-too-big`; a timer ends a tunnel with Close 1001 at a frame boundary; `ws_ping_ms` (0 = off) Pings a silent client and `ws_pong_ms` bounds the answer (`ws.pong-timeout`); `ws_close_ms` bounds the wait for a Close's answer. The upstream never sees the gateway's Pings. Not done: permessage-deflate, OCPP message validation. The access-log line of a tunnel is written when it ends and carries `"upgrade":"websocket"` and, if the tunnel saw a Close frame, `"ws_close":<code>` last.
- JWT (docs/jwt.md): a route sets `auth = "jwt"` (or `["api-key", "jwt"]`), `jwt_keys` (names; default all), `jwt_aud` and `jwt_iss` (exact; optional), `jwt_leeway` (0 to 60 seconds, default 0) and `auth_forward`. Keys are `[[jwt_key]]` tables with a `name` (the `kid`) and the Ed25519 `public_key` (43 characters of base64url; `python3 scripts/mkjwt.py keygen <name>` prints the table and the seed once on standard error): public keys are compiled in, nothing secret is. The only algorithm is `EdDSA`, never chosen from the token (`alg: none` and an HS256 token signed with the public key are `jwt.alg`); `exp` is required; a token is a compact JWS read by a bounded strict parser (3 segments, base64url without padding, 2,048 bytes, no repeated name, nesting 4). Every invalid token is the same `401` (`auth.invalid`, `error="invalid_token"`); the cause is in the access log's `rule` (`jwt.*`) and the per-route `jwt_refused` counters. The signature is checked last and costs about 5 ms: the loop is single threaded, so a flood of well-formed tokens is expensive (docs/jwt.md section 9). The log's `identity` is the name of the verifying key. `rate_key = "auth"` is refused on a route that takes tokens. No HS256, no JWKS, no revocation, no `sub` logging.
- Rate limiting (docs/ratelimit.md): a route sets `rate_limit = "100/s"` (`N/s`, `N/m` or `N/h`), `rate_burst`, `rate_key` (`route`, `header:<Name>`, `xff:last`, `xff:first`) and `rate_buckets`. A token bucket per key in a table of fixed size; past the limit the answer is `429` with `Retry-After` and the rule `limit.rate` (or `limit.rate-table` when the table has no bucket for a new key), and the request never reaches the upstream. There is no per-client-address key: the compiler gives no peer address. A header key is only as strong as the header (a client can rotate it); `route` is a hard ceiling on the upstream. Counters per route: `rate_limited`, `rate_table_full`.
- Authentication (docs/auth.md): a route sets `auth = "api-key"`, optionally `auth_header` (default `Authorization`, read as `Bearer <key>`; any other name is read as the whole value), `auth_keys` (names; default all) and `auth_forward` (default false: the credential header is removed before the upstream sees the request). Keys are `[[api_key]]` tables with a `name` and the `sha256` of the key (made by `python3 scripts/mkkey.py <name>`, which prints the key once on standard error): the binary holds digests, never a key, and compares a request's credential with every one of them with no early exit. Refusals: `auth.missing`, `auth.malformed` (a header twice, empty, another scheme, over 256 bytes), `auth.invalid` (all 401 with `WWW-Authenticate`) and `auth.forbidden` (403: a valid key the route does not allow). It is decided after routing and before the rate limit, the WebSocket checks and the dial. The access log adds `"identity":"<key name>"` last, only for a request that authenticated; `rate_key = "auth"` limits per identity; `cancho_gateway_auth_refused_total{route,kind}` counts refusals. A deployment with an `auth` route and a plain `listen` is refused unless `auth_allow_plain = true`: a key on plain HTTP is readable on the path. No JWT, no key change without a restart, no client certificates, no key in the query string.
- TLS cost (docs/tls.md section 12, docs/bench.md section 11; measured 2026-10-12): there is no client keep-alive, so every HTTPS request is a full handshake, 5.9 ms of CPU; one core serves about 157 HTTPS requests a second against 26,991 plain (1 in 170), and the default `tls_rate` of 50 a second caps it lower. An established connection costs 3.6 times the plain CPU per byte; the gateway's connections do not stay open.
- The authority report (files: read-only, and only the TLS certificate directory and /dev/urandom when tls_listen is set; foreign calls: none) is committed in `manifests/` and checked in CI. The network bound is not narrowed: the upstream set is enforced in code and tested, not proved by the compiler.

## Not built
HS256 and any algorithm but EdDSA, JWKS fetching, revocation, claims-based authorisation, the token's subject in the log or as a rate key (docs/jwt.md; EdDSA JWTs are built), a key change without a restart, client certificates, a rate limit keyed by client address (impossible: the compiler gives no peer address; a route, header or X-Forwarded-For key is built: docs/ratelimit.md), TLS certificate reload (TLS 1.3 itself is built: docs/tls.md), permessage-deflate and OCPP-J message validation on WebSocket tunnels (the handshake, the frame parser, the message limit, UTF-8, the keepalive Ping and the Close handshake are built: docs/websocket.md, docs/websocket-frames.md; at most 127 tunnels), client keep-alive, hot reload.
